definition: The right to come first because something is judged more important or higher in rank.
example: When the two club rules conflict, the newer one takes precedence.
nuance: Precedence means being first in importance or order; a precedent is an earlier case used as a model for later ones.
prompt: An emergency room nurse decides which patients to see first.
options: Patients with severe injuries take precedence over those with minor cuts.
The nurse treated a sprained ankle first because the chest pain took precedence.
Last year's flu outbreak set a precedence for how the ward handles crowds.
The nurse showed great precedence by staying calm during the busy shift.
reasons: The most urgent cases rightly come before less serious ones, which is the idea of ranking first.
If the chest pain came first in importance, it should have been treated first; the logic is reversed.
An earlier event that serves as a model is a precedent, not a precedence.
The word names an order of importance, not a personal quality like composure or poise.

practice.prompt: A student has an essay due tomorrow and a club meeting tonight.
options: The precedence of the meeting was a classroom on the library's second floor.
With the essay due tomorrow, it took precedence over the chess club meeting.
She gave the club meeting precedence, so she skipped it to work on her essay.
Her older brother's study habits became a precedence she decided to follow.
reasons: The word refers to rank or order of importance, not to a location.
The urgent deadline made the essay more important, so it came before the meeting.
Skipping the meeting shows the essay came first, which contradicts giving the meeting priority.
A past example someone copies is a precedent; this sentence mixes up the look-alike words.
